newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan dept store sales fall, reflect weak economy.
newsitem.headline: Japan dept store sales fall, reflect weak economy.

text.p: Sales at Japanese department stores fell for the fourth consecutive month in July, signalling that the nation's economy is still weak and in danger of slipping back, economists said on Friday.
The Japan Department Stores Association said on Friday that sales at department stores in Tokyo dropped 5.7 percent in July from a year earlier to 231.6 billion yen ($1.96 billion).

Department store sales in the Osaka area, the nation's second-largest commercial centre, fell 4.2 percent year-on-year to 154.6 billion yen ($1.31 billion) in July, the Kinki Department Stores Association said. Department stores in Japan are centred in the Tokyo and Osaka areas.

"It tells you that the economy is in quite a bit of trouble. I think it tells us that the government misjudged the impact of the consumption tax rise," said Richard Jerram, chief economist at ING Barings in Tokyo.
"It's going to be touch-and-go whether the economy goes into recession or not, but it's likely to just about avoid it," he added.
The Japanese government raised the national consumption tax to five percent from three percent in April.

Household spending, a major barometer for private consumption, fell 4.7 percent in June in real terms from a year earlier to an average 310,990 yen ($2,627) per household, the Management and Coordination Agency said earlier this month.
"The situation continued to be tough in July (at stores). Individual consumer demand showed only a weak recovery and corporate demand remained low," the Japan Department Stores Association said.
Sales in the Tokyo area have fallen on a year-on-year basis every month since April, after surging in March ahead of the consumption tax increase.
The association said that the dampening effect of the tax rise was lingering and that consumer purchases at summer clearance sales in the second half of the month were sluggish.
Sales of seasonal gifts were also slow, the association said.

This year's cancellation of special tax breaks also hit sales, analysts said. A special income tax break for individuals was introduced a few years ago to encourage consumption, but the government decided to do away with it this year as part of its fiscal tightening measures.
In addition, bad weather, including a series of typhoons, discouraged shoppers in July, said a spokesman at department store operator Mitsukoshi Ltd .
"Our sales in July fell five percent year-on-year. We think sales will continue to be dull after August," he added.
"We cannot expect much of a recovery in the autumn," added a spokesman for Isetan Co Ltd .

Kazutoshi Aratake, an economist at the Nikko Research Center, said the situation will not improve during the current business year, as consumers may tighten their purse strings as they face greater financial burdens without the help of government subsidies.

"Sales will not recover during this business year due to the effects of the cancellation of the special tax reduction in June and an increase in individual medical costs scheduled to take effect in September," he said.
Japanese workers will be required to bear a heavier part of their medical costs from September as part of the government's plan to cut overall spending.
Some analysts, however, were more optimistic, predicting that sales should start picking up as early as the autumn if the weather improves.

"Sales are likely to increase on a year-on-year basis around October, as long as there are no typhoons hitting Japan on weekends and the winter is not as warm as it was last year," said Futoshi Saito, an analyst at Daiwa Research Institute. ($1=118 yen)
